summary: Describes an RTP payload format for the High Quality profile of the SMPTE VC-2 video standard (ST 2042-1). It enables low-complexity, high-bandwidth streaming of lossless or lossy compressed video.

eli5.summary: This explains how to cut a high-quality video into small parcels for the internet and put it back together at the other end.

questions: what is the video/vc2 media type
why does vc-2 rtp extend the sequence number
subtitle: How to carry lossless or lightly compressed VC-2 HQ professional video in RTP packets at gigabit rates.

tldr.problem: VC-2 is a low-latency, low-complexity video codec for professional use, and its streams have to be cut into network packets without losing the structure the decoder needs.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP packet carries one Parse Info Header's data unit (a sequence header, a picture fragment, auxiliary data, padding or an end-of-sequence marker), identified by a Parse Code, with the sequence number extended to 32 bits.
tldr.outcome: The receiver rebuilds a valid VC-2 sequence from the packets. The payload is registered as the video/vc2 media type.

today: RFC 8450 is a Proposed Standard from October 2018 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The VC-2 Codec and Its Use
sections.content:
This RFC specifies an RTP payload format for SMPTE ST 2042-1:2017, known as VC-2, specifically its High Quality (HQ) profile. VC-2 is a wavelet-based codec aimed at professional video with high bit-rates and only low levels of compression.

It is designed for low complexity and potentially very low latency through both encoder and decoder, possibly as low as a few lines of video. The price is that it lacks many of the more powerful compression techniques of other codecs, so it suits coded data rates around half to a quarter of uncompressed video at similar visual quality. The primary use is likely to be professional video production.
sections.eli5: It is a video squeezer that squeezes only a little, so pictures stay very sharp and the squeezing is quick.

sections.title: How a VC-2 Stream Is Built
sections.content:
A VC-2 Stream is made of one or more Sequences, each independently decodable. A Sequence is a series of 13-octet Parse Info Headers, each followed by a variable-length Data Unit, and it begins and ends with a Parse Info Header. The header says what type of Data Unit comes next.

The HQ profile allows only Sequence Headers, High Quality Pictures, High Quality Fragments, Auxiliary Data, Padding Data and End of Sequence. A picture holds parameters followed by Coded Slices, each a rectangular region of the transformed picture. Fragments carry the same data in smaller units, and this payload format uses Fragments, not whole pictures.

Sequences can be joined in the middle, so a receiver should not assume the first Data Unit it sees is a Sequence Header.
sections.eli5: A video is a long string of beads. Each bead has a small tag saying what kind of bead it is, and the tags tell the player how to use it.

sections.title: Packet Types and Payload Header
sections.content:
Each RTP packet carries data for a single Parse Info Header and its Data Unit. A Data Unit must not be split across packets, with one exception: an Auxiliary Data Unit may span packets, marked with the B and E flags. Pictures are sent as equivalent sets of Fragments sized to fit the network MTU.

Six packet types exist: Sequence Header, Transform Parameters fragment, Coded Slices fragment, End of Sequence, Auxiliary Data and Padding. They are told apart by the PC (Parse Code) field, except the two fragment kinds, which share a PC and differ in No. of Slices (0 for transform parameters).

The extended header holds fields such as Extended Sequence Number, Picture Number, Slice Prefix Bytes, Slice Size Scaler, Fragment Length, No. of Slices and Slice Offset X and Y. The I flag marks data from a field of an interlaced frame and F marks the second field. All multi-bit fields are unsigned integers in network byte order.
sections.eli5: Each parcel has a label on the front saying what is inside, which picture it belongs to and where its piece goes.

sections.title: RTP Header Usage and Sequencing Rules
sections.content:
The marker bit MUST be set on a packet holding the final slice of a coded picture and not otherwise. The payload type is dynamically allocated. Because VC-2 data rates can be gigabits per second, the 16-bit RTP sequence number would cycle very fast, so the sequence number is extended to 32 bits: the RTP field holds the low-order 16 bits and Extended Sequence Number holds the high-order 16 bits.

The timestamp is the sampling instant of the coded picture, and a 90kHz clock SHOULD be used. A packet must not hold data from more than one picture. A Sequence Header packet should share the timestamp of the picture that follows it, and an End of Sequence packet that of the previous picture.

The sender MUST send at least one transform-parameters packet per picture, may repeat it with identical data, and MUST NOT start a new picture before finishing the current one. If a receiver gets slices without parameters, it may assume the parameters are unchanged (possibly giving malformed pictures) or discard the picture (dropped frames).
sections.eli5: Parcels are numbered so they can be put in order. Because so many are sent so fast, the numbers need extra digits so they do not run out and repeat.

sections.title: Stream Constraints and Reassembly
sections.content:
Only parse codes 0x00, 0x10, 0x20, 0x30 and 0xEC may appear in a stream sent this way. Every HQ Picture Fragment MUST be no longer than 65535 bytes, must use Slice Prefix Bytes and Slice Size Scaler no greater than 65535, and SHOULD fit in the network MTU. A stream with whole HQ Pictures (0xE8) can be converted by splitting them, provided no single slice is too large. Otherwise it must be re-encoded.

To rebuild a VC-2 Sequence, the receiver prepends a valid 13-octet Parse Info Header to each packet's data, with the same parse code, and fills in the next and previous parse offsets. Sequence Headers must appear before the pictures that follow them. Fragments with the same picture number may be combined into one picture (0xE8), and that MUST be done if the stream must comply with major versions 1 or 2 of VC-2. Auxiliary Data is reassembled using the B and E bits and padding is a series of zero bytes.
sections.eli5: The rules say how big each parcel may be. At the other end, you glue the right labels back on and stack the parcels in order to get the whole video again.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Mapping
sections.content:
The payload is identified by the media type video/vc2. The required parameters are rate (the RTP timestamp clock rate, SHOULD be 90000) and profile (only HQ is allowed). Optional parameters are version (only 3 is allowed, since HQ Picture Fragments require it) and level (any integer).

In SDP, the type goes in the m= line, the subtype and rate go in a=rtpmap, and profile, version and level go in a=fmtp as semicolon-separated pairs. In the RFC's example, level 0 means unknown or non-standard level. Offer/answer is simple: all parameters are declarative. IANA has registered video/vc2 in the "RTP Payload Format Media Types" registry. The type is only defined for transfer via RTP.
sections.eli5: The name tag for this kind of video says what it is and how fast its clock ticks, so both ends agree before they start.

sections.title: Error Correction and Congestion Control
sections.content:
VC-2 has no built-in protection against loss, so Forward Error Correction from RFC 5109 may be used. For multilevel protection, packets SHOULD be assigned to layers by importance: Sequence Headers, then Transform Parameters fragments, then Coded Slices fragments, then Auxiliary Data and End of Sequence, then Padding. Padding SHOULD NOT be protected.

Congestion control follows RFC 3550 and the RTP profile in use. Users on best-effort service MUST monitor packet loss, and implementations MUST comply with the circuit breakers of RFC 8083. The RFC warns that data rates are likely in the gigabits per second range, which may be fine on a correctly provisioned closed network, but data could get out onto the open internet.
sections.eli5: The most important parcels get the most spare copies. And because so many parcels fly out so fast, you must watch that you are not flooding the road.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The usual RTP security considerations apply, and the RFC says choosing confidentiality, integrity and source authentication belongs to whoever uses RTP, who SHOULD use strong security mechanisms. The payload format has no notable non-uniform receiver complexity, so it is unlikely to enable denial of service through pathological data, and it has no active content.

To avoid buffer overruns, a receiver MUST consider both the reported Fragment length and the actual received size of a packet with slice data. A transmitter that decodes variable-length coded headers to extract data could also face buffer overruns if it is not careful.
sections.eli5: Check that each parcel really is as big as its label says before you unpack it.

data.code:

a=rtpmap:112 vc2/90000
a=fmtp:112 profile=HQ;version=3;level=0
